why: The gesture→action law of a domain-bound world viewport, written once and read by two implementations: the React `World3dHost` mounted in jsdom (🧪️tests/🖱️world3d-interaction) and the language-neutral Node oracle (`world3dPointerGestureOracle`, the react target's 📜️script.ts). Until this fixture existed the 6.4k-line host had only pure-function and SSR-snapshot coverage: nothing proved that a pick reaches `interactionSelect`, that a move reaches `interactionHover`, that a background click clears, that a completed orbit debounces into exactly one `setCamera`, or that a marquee release replaces the selection with the deduplicated topology targets.

gestures.why: A bare pick on a rendered instance selects the TOPOLOGY id the instance stands for (`interactionId`), never the render id, at object granularity.

Shift is the additive modifier, and the resolved `MergeMode` goes on the wire VERBATIM — no host-side translation. Live defect 2026-09-12 (`📓️selection-merge-vocabulary-2026-09-12.md`): the host translated `additive` into a private word `add`, which the framework's `parse_merge_mode` rejects, so every shift-click on this scene faulted with `interactionSelect: unknown merge 'add'`.
Ctrl (and cmd on macOS) is the subtractive modifier — `resolveWorldMergeMode` → `subtractive`, on the wire unchanged.
cmd is ctrl's platform twin — the SAME mode, so a macOS user and a Windows user select identically.
shift+ctrl is the invertive chord — the third multi-select word, and the last one the old `add`/`remove`/`toggle` translation could reach.

The scene renders ONE topology id as two instances. A single click on the second one selects that id ONCE — a selection is a set of topology ids, so a pick can never publish the same id twice (live defect 2026-09-12: the guest published selectedIds ["extrude@solid","extrude@solid"]).

The wire-args builder itself is the host's set boundary: handed the same topology id twice (two rendered instances of one channel, or a batch no caller ran through `interactionTargetsForInstances`), it emits ONE target. Proving it at the builder — not only at one call site — is what makes a duplicate unrepresentable on the host side.
Hover reports the scene's OWN declared granularity (`domainGranularityId`), not the object granularity a pick uses, and travels on the `pointer` channel.
A click that hits no instance clears the domain selection — an EMPTY target list at the scene granularity, never a missing dispatch.

Orbit/pan/zoom drives the local rig every frame; only the COMPLETED gesture crosses to the guest, trailing-debounced so a wheel burst costs one dispatch, and the pose nests under `camera` (never spread flat beside `windowId`).
A marquee release always REPLACES, and several rendered instances of one channel collapse onto that channel's single topology target (`interactionTargetsForInstances` dedup).

wiring.why: Source-level anchors the Node oracle re-checks so a refactor cannot quietly move a gesture onto a different verb while the mounted suite still passes on a stale mock.
